q.intro.text: A pizza is twelve inches across. How much cheese covers the top? That is the pizza's area, in square inches.

q.ask.text: Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Let's work it out in four steps. Press each one, and watch the picture first.

e.step0.text: The radius goes from the center to the crust. It is half of the twelve inches across: six inches.

e.step1.text: Cut the pizza into sixteen wedges and lay them in a row, one up, one down. The crust is the circumference: pi times twelve, twelve pi inches. Half of it runs along the top: six pi.

e.step2.text: The same cheese now makes an almost rectangle, six pi long and six tall. A wedge's side is the radius. The area is six pi times six: thirty-six pi square inches. That is pi times r squared.

e.step3.text: Thirty-six pi is about thirty-six times three point one four: about one hundred thirteen square inches. Check: the shape holds about three squares of six by six, and three times thirty-six is one hundred eight. Close.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the long side six pi, not twelve pi?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Half the wedges have their crust on top, half at the bottom. The top gets half the circumference.

e.why.all.text: The whole crust is twelve pi, but only half of it is on top. The other half runs along the bottom. So the long side is six pi.

e.why.d.text: Twelve inches is the way across. The top is made of crust, half the way around: six pi, about nineteen inches.

t.intro.text: Now a round rug, ten feet across. How much floor does it cover? The first two steps are done for you.

t.given.text: The radius is ten divided by two, five feet. The edge of the rug is pi times ten, ten pi feet. Watch the wedges.

t.sides.text: How long is the top of the near rectangle, and how tall is it?

t.sides.ok.text: Yes. The top is half the edge, five pi feet, and the height is the radius, five feet.

t.sides.half.text: The whole edge is ten pi, but the top only gets half of it. The other half runs along the bottom.

t.sides.d.text: The height is the side of one wedge, from the center to the edge. That is the radius, not the diameter.

t.sides.other.text: The top is half of ten pi. The height is the side of one wedge, the radius.

t.area.text: So what is the area, in terms of pi?

t.area.ok.text: Yes. Five pi times five is twenty-five pi square feet. That is pi times five squared.

t.area.pow.text: Five squared means five times five, not five times two. Long side times height: five pi times five.

t.area.d.text: That squares the diameter, ten. The height of the shape is the radius, five.

t.area.half.text: Use the top, five pi, not the whole edge, ten pi. Five pi times five.

t.area.other.text: The area is the long side times the height: five pi times five.

t.round.text: About how many square feet is that? Use three point one four for pi.

t.round.c.text: Thirty-one point four is ten pi, the edge around the rug. The floor it covers is the area, twenty-five pi.

t.round.sq.text: That squares pi too. Only the radius is squared: twenty-five times three point one four.

t.round.three.text: Seventy-five is the quick estimate with pi as three. With three point one four it is a bit more.

t.round.other.text: Multiply twenty-five by three point one four.

t.done.text: Twenty-five pi is about twenty-five times three point one four: seventy-eight point five square feet. Check: about three times twenty-five is seventy-five. Close.

t.cb.rr.text: At the start you picked thirty-six square inches. That is six times six, one square of side r. The pizza holds about three point one four of those squares: about one hundred thirteen.

t.cb.c.text: At the start you picked about thirty-eight. That is pi times twelve, the crust, a length around the edge. The cheese is an area: pi r squared, thirty-six pi, about one hundred thirteen.

t.cb.right.text: At the start you picked about one hundred thirteen square inches, and that was right: pi times six squared, thirty-six pi. Now you know why.

t.cb.none.text: At the start: the twelve inch pizza has thirty-six pi, about one hundred thirteen square inches of cheese.

t.sure.0.text: You were guessing then. Now you can explain it.

p.intro.text: Sam says: a sixteen inch pizza is twice as wide as an eight inch pizza. So two eight inch pizzas are as much pizza as one sixteen inch pizza. Is Sam right?

p.build.text: Prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.no.k.text: That is Sam's idea. The width is times two, but the area uses r twice: two times two is four.

p.no.pi.text: Pi is the same for every circle, about three point one four, big or small.

p.no.add.text: Sizes are multiplied, not added. The radius is times two, not plus four.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. Sixteen divided by eight is two. The radii, four and eight inches: times two.

p.c2.text: The crust is two pi r. Double r, double the crust: eight pi becomes sixteen pi.

p.c3.text: But the area is pi r squared, and r is used twice: two times two is four. Sixteen pi becomes sixty-four pi. Four small pizzas fit the big one's box the same way.

p.c4.text: Two small pizzas are only thirty-two pi. It takes four to match sixty-four pi. Sam is wrong.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Each line has its reason, and the picture backs every one. Lengths double, and the area is four times as big.
